sections.title: What are 2D Arrays / Matrices?
sections.content:
A **matrix** is an array of arrays: each element `matrix[row][col]` is accessed by two indices. But working with matrices requires more than just knowing the syntax - it requires a mental model shift. A 2D structure has spatial properties that 1D arrays lack: rows, columns, diagonals, and boundaries. The key discipline is keeping straight which index is which.

In JavaScript, `matrix[i][j]` means: the `i`-th sub-array (row), then the `j`-th element in that row (column). `i` moves vertically (down), `j` moves horizontally (right). This is the **row-major** convention. It's opposite to Cartesian coordinates where `x` (horizontal) comes first - a persistent source of bugs.

Real uses of matrices span many domains. **Grid problems** model game boards, mazes, and maps as matrices where each cell has coordinates. **Image processing** represents a greyscale image as a matrix of pixel intensities. **Graph adjacency matrices** encode edges between nodes. **DP tables** use a 2D matrix to store subproblem results for problems with two varying parameters.

The techniques from 1D arrays extend cleanly: traversal becomes 2D traversal, prefix sums become 2D prefix sums, and BFS/DFS on arrays becomes BFS/DFS on grids. Each technique adds one dimension of complexity but uses the same underlying logic.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Matrix techniques apply whenever data has a 2D spatial structure or whenever two independent indices define a state. Grid problems are the most common: islands, paths, and shortest routes in a grid all need 2D traversal and BFS/DFS. When the problem says 'm × n' you are working with a matrix. Rotation, transposition, and spiral traversal are matrix-specific operations that appear frequently in interviews.

Core Template
sections.explanation: Grid BFS visits cells level by level from a source, marking visited before enqueuing to prevent duplicate processing. The 2D prefix sum enables O(1) rectangle sum queries after O(mn) construction using inclusion-exclusion to avoid double-counting.

items.name: 8-Directional Grid
items.description: Add the four diagonal directions `[[1,1],[1,-1],[-1,1],[-1,-1]]` to the directions array. Used in problems where diagonal movement is allowed (chess-style). Boundary checks remain the same.

items.name: Multi-Source BFS
items.description: When you need the distance from the nearest source cell (e.g., nearest 0 in a matrix of 0s and 1s), enqueue ALL source cells at the start with distance 0, then run BFS normally. Each cell is reached by the nearest source first due to BFS level-order property.

items.name: Grid with Obstacles
items.description: Add a condition to skip blocked cells during BFS/DFS expansion. Instead of just checking `!visited[nr][nc]`, also check `grid[nr][nc] !== obstacle`. Path-finding and flood fill problems use this variant.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(m×n) for traversal and BFS/DFS, O(m×n) for 2D prefix build
sections.space: O(m×n) for visited array and 2D prefix sum
sections.explanation: Every cell is visited at most once in BFS/DFS (due to the visited check), giving O(mn) time and O(mn) space for the visited array. The 2D prefix sum requires one pass over all mn cells to build, and O(mn) extra space for the prefix array - both unavoidable since every cell contributes to some rectangle query.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Row vs column index confusion: `matrix[row][col]` has `row` as the vertical index (0 = top) and `col` as the horizontal index (0 = left). This is opposite to Cartesian (x, y) coordinates where x is horizontal first. Writing `matrix[col][row]` reads the transposed matrix and produces wrong results.

Mutating the grid as a visited marker without resetting: marking cells as visited by modifying the grid (e.g., `grid[r][c] = '0'`) is a common shortcut but fails when the same grid is used for multiple BFS calls or when the original grid is needed for subsequent operations.

Missing boundary checks before array access: accessing `matrix[r][c]` without checking `r >= 0 && r < m && c >= 0 && c < n` first throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined' or silently reads `undefined`. Always check bounds before accessing.

Marking visited after dequeue instead of before enqueue: if you mark visited when a cell is popped from the queue, the same cell can be enqueued multiple times (once from each neighbor that reaches it), causing exponential work and incorrect distances in BFS.
